# Probability Distributions and Sampling ##### Why the average of anything is bell-shaped A logistics analyst in Surat plotted delivery times for 200,000 orders. The shape was violently right-skewed — most deliveries in 20–40 minutes, a long tail stretching past three hours. Nothing bell-shaped about it. Then she plotted something different: she took random samples of 30 deliveries, computed each sample's **average**, and plotted 5,000 of those averages. It was a near-perfect bell curve. She had accidentally demonstrated the Central Limit Theorem — the result that makes most of applied statistics work. It says that no matter how strange the underlying distribution, the distribution of *sample means* becomes approximately normal as sample size grows. That single fact is why you can put a confidence interval on an average, why A/B tests work, and why the normal distribution shows up everywhere even though almost nothing in nature is actually normal. ##### Discrete vs continuous A **discrete** random variable takes countable values — number of orders, defect count, dice outcome. Its **probability mass function** (PMF) gives the probability of each exact value, and `P(X = 3)` is a meaningful question. A **continuous** variable takes any value in a range — delivery time, temperature, weight. Its **probability density function** (PDF) gives density, not probability, and `P(X = 34.7 exactly)` is zero. You can only ask about intervals: `P(30 < X < 40)`. Both have a **cumulative distribution function** (CDF): `F(x) = P(X ≤ x)`. The CDF is what you actually use in practice — for percentiles, p-values and tail probabilities. ```python import numpy as np from scipy import stats import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid") # Discrete: PMF gives exact-value probability print(stats.binom.pmf(k=3, n=10, p=0.3)) # P(exactly 3 successes) = 0.2668 # Continuous: PDF is density, CDF gives interval probability print(stats.norm.pdf(x=0, loc=0, scale=1)) # 0.3989 — a density, not a probability print(stats.norm.cdf(1.96) - stats.norm.cdf(-1.96)) # 0.95 — this IS a probability ``` ##### The three distributions you must know **Binomial** — the number of successes in `n` independent trials, each with probability `p`. Use it when: counting successes out of a fixed number of attempts. How many of 500 emails get opened? How many of 200 applicants are approved? ```python n, p = 500, 0.22 # 500 emails, 22% open rate dist = stats.binom(n, p) print(f"mean: {dist.mean():.1f}") # n*p = 110 print(f"std: {dist.std():.2f}") # sqrt(n*p*(1-p)) = 9.26 print(f"P(exactly 110): {dist.pmf(110):.4f}") print(f"P(at most 100): {dist.cdf(100):.4f}") print(f"P(more than 130): {1 - dist.cdf(130):.4f}") print(f"90% interval: {dist.ppf(0.05)} to {dist.ppf(0.95)}") # ppf = inverse CDF ``` Conditions: fixed `n`, two outcomes, constant `p`, independent trials. That last one is often violated — if one customer's purchase influences another's, binomial understates the variance. **Poisson** — the number of events in a fixed interval, given an average rate `λ`. Use it when: counting occurrences in time or space with no fixed maximum. Support tickets per hour, defects per batch, accidents per month. ```python lam = 4.5 # average 4.5 tickets per hour dist = stats.poisson(lam) print(f"mean = variance = {dist.mean()}") # a defining property of Poisson print(f"P(no tickets): {dist.pmf(0):.4f}") print(f"P(8 or more): {1 - dist.cdf(7):.4f}") # staffing question ``` The distinctive property: **mean equals variance**. If your count data has variance much larger than its mean, it is *overdispersed* and Poisson is the wrong model — a real and common finding. Poisson is the limit of the binomial when `n` is large and `p` is small, with `λ = n·p`. That is why rare events in large populations follow it. **Normal (Gaussian)** — the bell curve, defined by mean `μ` and standard deviation `σ`. ```python mu, sigma = 34.0, 8.5 # delivery minutes dist = stats.norm(mu, sigma) print(f"P(under 25 min): {dist.cdf(25):.4f}") print(f"P(25 to 45 min): {dist.cdf(45) - dist.cdf(25):.4f}") print(f"95th percentile: {dist.ppf(0.95):.1f} min") # SLA planning ``` | Distribution | Models | Parameters | Key property | |---|---|---|---| | Binomial | Successes in n trials | n, p | Fixed maximum | | Poisson | Events per interval | λ | mean = variance | | Normal | Continuous measurements, sums, averages | μ, σ | Symmetric, CLT limit | | Exponential | Time between Poisson events | λ | Memoryless | | Lognormal | Positive, right-skewed (income, prices) | μ, σ of log | log is normal | | Uniform | Equally likely in a range | a, b | Flat | ##### The 68-95-99.7 rule For any normal distribution: ``` 68% ┌─────────┐ 95% ┌──────────────┐ 99.7% ┌────────────────────┐ μ-3σ μ-2σ μ-σ μ μ+σ μ+2σ μ+3σ ``` ```python mu, sigma = 34.0, 8.5 for k in (1, 2, 3): p = stats.norm.cdf(mu + k*sigma, mu, sigma) - stats.norm.cdf(mu - k*sigma, mu, sigma) print(f"±{k}σ [{mu-k*sigma:5.1f}, {mu+k*sigma:5.1f}] contains {p:.1%}") ``` A **z-score** expresses any value in standard deviations from the mean: `z = (x − μ) / σ`. It makes different scales comparable — a z of 2.1 means the same thing whether the units are rupees, minutes or kilograms. The critical caveat: **this rule only applies to approximately normal data.** Applying "3 sigma = outlier" to income, which is lognormal, flags perfectly ordinary high earners. Always check the shape first. ##### Sampling and sampling distributions You almost never measure a whole population; you measure a **sample** and infer. The vocabulary matters. A **parameter** describes the population (μ, σ) and is unknown. A **statistic** describes your sample (x̄, s) and is what you compute. The **sampling distribution** is the distribution of a statistic across all possible samples — and understanding it is the whole basis of inference. ```python rng = np.random.default_rng(42) population = rng.lognormal(mean=3.4, sigma=0.55, size=200_000) # skewed delivery times print(f"population mean: {population.mean():.2f}") # One sample of 50 gives one estimate — and it is not the truth one = rng.choice(population, size=50) print(f"one sample mean: {one.mean():.2f}") # Repeat 5000 times: this is the sampling distribution means = np.array([rng.choice(population, 50).mean() for _ in range(5000)]) print(f"mean of sample means: {means.mean():.2f}") # ≈ population mean print(f"std of sample means: {means.std():.3f}") # the STANDARD ERROR print(f"theoretical SE: {population.std() / np.sqrt(50):.3f}") ``` The **standard error** is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution: `SE = σ / √n`. That formula contains the most practically important trade-off in statistics. Because of the square root, **halving your uncertainty requires quadrupling your sample size.** Going from 100 to 400 observations halves the standard error; going from 400 to 800 barely helps. This is why survey costs escalate and why A/B tests need so much traffic. Sampling methods matter too: **simple random** (everyone equally likely), **stratified** (sample within groups to guarantee representation — essential when a subgroup is small), **cluster** (sample whole groups, cheaper but less precise), and **convenience** (whoever is available — the source of most bad survey data). Selection bias from non-random sampling cannot be fixed by increasing the sample size. ##### The Central Limit Theorem **As sample size increases, the distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution — regardless of the population's shape.** ```python population = rng.exponential(scale=30, size=500_000) # heavily right-skewed fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 3.8)) axes[0].hist(population, bins=60, color="#e53e3e", alpha=0.8) axes[0].set_title(f"Population (skew {stats.skew(population):.2f})") for ax, n in zip(axes[1:], [5, 30, 100]): means = np.array([rng.choice(population, n).mean() for _ in range(4000)]) ax.hist(means, bins=45, color="#3182ce", alpha=0.85, density=True) xs = np.linspace(means.min(), means.max(), 200) ax.plot(xs, stats.norm.pdf(xs, population.mean(), population.std()/np.sqrt(n)), "k--", lw=1.5) ax.set_title(f"n = {n} (skew {stats.skew(means):.2f})") fig.tight_layout() ``` Watch the skewness numbers collapse toward zero as `n` grows. That is the CLT happening. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Any population shape:
skewed, bimodal, uniform] --> B[Take a sample of size n] B --> C[Compute its mean] C --> D[Repeat many times] D --> E[Distribution of those means
is approximately Normal] E --> F[Centre = population mean] E --> G[Spread = sigma / sqrt n] ``` Three things the CLT does **not** say, each a common misreading: - It does not say your *data* becomes normal. Individual delivery times stay skewed forever. - It does not work for every statistic. Sample means and sums converge; the maximum does not. - "n ≥ 30 is enough" is a rule of thumb, not a law. Mildly skewed data converges by n = 15; extremely skewed or heavy-tailed data may need several hundred. Why it matters: because sample means are normal, you can compute confidence intervals and p-values using normal theory, whatever the raw data looks like. Every t-test and A/B test you run tomorrow rests on this. ##### Fitting a distribution to real data ```python data = df["delivery_min"].dropna().values # Visual check first fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5)) sns.histplot(data, bins=50, stat="density", ax=axes[0], color="#4299e1") xs = np.linspace(data.min(), data.max(), 300) for name, dist in [("normal", stats.norm), ("lognormal", stats.lognorm), ("gamma", stats.gamma)]: params = dist.fit(data) axes[0].plot(xs, dist.pdf(xs, *params), lw=2, label=name) axes[0].legend(); axes[0].set_title("Candidate fits") # Q-Q plot: the honest diagnostic stats.probplot(data, dist="lognorm", sparams=stats.lognorm.fit(data), plot=axes[1]) axes[1].set_title("Q-Q plot — points on the line means a good fit") fig.tight_layout() # Formal test (use with care) print(stats.kstest(data, "lognorm", args=stats.lognorm.fit(data))) ``` The **Q-Q plot** is the diagnostic to trust. If the points follow the diagonal, the distribution fits; systematic curvature at the ends means the tails are wrong, which is usually what matters most. Formal goodness-of-fit tests are less useful than they appear: with 200,000 rows, any test rejects any distribution, because no real data is exactly anything. Use the plot, and remember George Box — all models are wrong, some are useful. ##### Common mistakes - Assuming data is normal without plotting it. - Applying the 68-95-99.7 rule or 3-sigma outlier detection to skewed data. - Using Poisson for overdispersed counts without checking mean against variance. - Believing the CLT makes your raw data normal. - Treating `n ≥ 30` as a guarantee rather than a rough guide. - Confusing standard deviation (spread of data) with standard error (spread of the estimate). - Expecting linear returns from more data, when precision improves as `√n`. - Reading a PDF value as a probability. - Using a goodness-of-fit p-value on a huge sample and rejecting a perfectly usable model. - Convenience sampling and assuming a bigger sample fixes the bias. It does not. ##### Hands-on Generate and plot normal, binomial and Poisson distributions with `scipy.stats`, varying the parameters and observing how each changes shape — in particular, watch the binomial approach a normal shape as `n` grows, and Poisson approach normal as `λ` grows. Then build the CLT demonstration: start from a heavily skewed population, draw thousands of samples at n = 2, 5, 30 and 100, plot the distribution of sample means at each, and print the skewness so you can see it collapse numerically as well as visually. Overlay the theoretical normal curve using `σ/√n` and confirm it matches. For the mini-project, build an interactive notebook using `ipywidgets` sliders that lets you vary distribution parameters and see the shape update live, alongside a CLT demonstration with an adjustable sample size and population shape. The value is in the intuition — being able to drag `n` from 2 to 200 and watch the bell curve form makes the theorem permanent in a way that reading about it does not. For the assignment, take a real column from a dataset, decide which distribution best describes it, and justify the choice with a histogram overlaid with the fitted theoretical curve plus a Q-Q plot. Be honest in your write-up: state where the fit is good and where it breaks down. Most real data fits nothing perfectly, and saying "lognormal fits the body well but underestimates the extreme tail" is a better answer than claiming a perfect match. ##### Key takeaways - Discrete distributions give probability at exact values; continuous ones give density, and only intervals have probability. - Binomial for successes in fixed trials, Poisson for events per interval (check mean = variance), normal for measurements and averages. - The standard error is `σ/√n`, so halving uncertainty costs four times the data. - The CLT makes sample *means* normal regardless of population shape — it does not normalise your raw data. - Judge distribution fit with a Q-Q plot, not a p-value, and expect real data to fit approximately at best.
